# The Rise and Fall of the Belmont Glass Works: An Industrial and Artistic History of Bellaire’s Pioneer Glasshouse (1866–1890)
## 1\. Introduction: The Geopolitical and Industrial Crucible of the Upper Ohio Valley
The history of the American glass industry in the latter half of the 19th century is a narrative defined by the interplay of geology, transportation, and skilled migration. While New England and Pittsburgh had established themselves as the antebellum centers of glass production, the post-Civil War era witnessed a dramatic westward shift of industrial capital. At the heart of this transformation was the Upper Ohio Valley, a region that offered a unique convergence of logistical and resource-based advantages. Within this burgeoning industrial corridor, the **Belmont Glass Works** (1866–1890) emerged not merely as a factory, but as a foundational institution that would catalyze the transformation of Bellaire, Ohio, into the renowned "Glass City" .

This report provides an exhaustive analysis of the Belmont Glass Works, tracing its evolution from a cooperative experiment known as **Barnes, Faupel & Co.** to its zenith as a premier manufacturer of Early American Pattern Glass (EAPG). Through a detailed examination of corporate records, patent filings, and material culture, we explore the technological innovations of its mold shop, the artistic merit of its patterns—most notably the "Royal" and "Daisy & Button" lines—and the macroeconomic forces of the "Gas Boom" that ultimately precipitated its dissolution. Furthermore, this study addresses and corrects persistent historical inaccuracies regarding pattern attribution, specifically the conflation of Belmont’s output with the "Racine" moniker, and documents the diaspora of its workforce, whose expertise would go on to seed the glass industries of Northwest Ohio and Indiana .

### 1.1 The Strategic Advantage of Bellaire
To understand the significance of Belmont Glass Works, one must first appreciate the strategic geography of Bellaire. Situated in Belmont County on the western bank of the Ohio River, directly opposite the industrial hub of Wheeling, West Virginia, Bellaire possessed the three critical ingredients for 19th-century heavy industry: fuel, sand, and transport.

1. **Bituminous Coal:** In the era prior to the widespread exploitation of natural gas, coal was the lifeblood of the glass furnace. Bellaire sat atop massive coal seams, allowing factories to mine fuel virtually on-site. This abundance of cheap thermal energy gave Bellaire a distinct cost advantage over eastern competitors who faced higher fuel transport costs . 
2. **The River and the Rail:** The Ohio River had long served as the primary artery for moving goods to the expanding markets of the South and West. However, it was the arrival of the railroads—specifically the Baltimore & Ohio (B\&O) and the Central Ohio Railroad—that integrated Bellaire into the national grid. The convergence of these lines allowed Belmont Glass Works to ship fragile tableware efficiently to growing urban centers like Chicago, St. Louis, and Cincinnati . 
3. **Human Capital:** The proximity to Wheeling, an established glass center, facilitated a cross-river exchange of talent. Skilled gaffers, blowers, and mold makers moved freely between the two cities, creating a dense network of technical expertise. It was from this rich labor pool that Belmont Glass Works would draw its founding cooperators .

### 1.2 The Genesis of an Industry
When Barnes, Faupel & Co. broke ground in 1866, they were not just building a factory; they were inaugurating an era. Belmont Glass Works was the first glasshouse in Bellaire and only the second in the entire county. Its success served as a proof of concept for the region. Following Belmont's establishment, capital flooded into the area, and by 1880, Belmont County had risen to rank sixth in the nation for glass manufacturing, with Ohio ranking fourth. By 1890, the year of Belmont's closure, the state had climbed to second place nationally in production value, a testament to the momentum initiated by this pioneer firm .

## ---

**2\. The Formative Years: From Cooperative Roots to Corporate Stability (1866–1870)**

### 2.1 Barnes, Faupel & Co.: The Cooperative Model
The enterprise was organized in August 1865 and commenced production in 1866 under the name **Barnes, Faupel & Co.**.2 The organizational structure of this early firm reflects a broader trend in the post-Civil War glass industry: the cooperative. In a capital-intensive industry where the gap between management and labor was often stark, the cooperative model allowed skilled artisans to pool their resources and labor to become owner-operators.

The founding group was a coalition of businessmen and craftsmen. **Henry Faupel** and **George Barnes** provided the titular leadership, but the roster of incorporators reveals the depth of practical glassmaking experience involved:

* **James S. Gill:** An English immigrant born in 1820, Gill had settled in Wheeling in the 1840s before crossing the river to help organize the Bellaire works. His technical knowledge was instrumental in the plant's design . 
* **Charles Henry Over, John Robinson, and John Crimmel:** These men were listed as "glass-blowers" in early directories, yet they were also incorporators. This dual status of worker-owner ensured that the production floor had a direct voice in corporate governance, a feature that likely contributed to the high quality of the company's early output .

### 2.2 The Trial by Fire: September 1867
The resilience of the fledgling company was tested early. In September 1867, barely a year after production began, the factory was consumed by fire . Fire was the scourge of the 19th-century glass industry. The combination of molten glass (2,400°F), coal-fired furnaces, wooden building frames, and packing materials like straw and hay created a perpetually high-risk environment.

The destruction of the physical plant could have easily bankrupted the young partnership. However, the partners' commitment to the venture was absolute. They mobilized capital and labor to rebuild immediately, and the works were back in operation by the spring of 1868 . This rapid recovery demonstrates both the financial solvency of the partners and the strong market demand for their products.

### 2.3 Incorporation and Restructuring (1868)
Following the reconstruction, the partnership was formalized into a corporation. In December 1868, the entity was chartered as the **Belmont Glass Works**.2 The slate of incorporators for this new legal entity included Henry Faupel, Levi Cassell, James S. Gill, Charles Henry Over, John Robinson, John Crimmel, and Thomas J. Fleming.

The leadership hierarchy in 1871 was established as follows:

* **President:** Henry Faupel 
* **Treasurer:** William Gorby 
* **Manager:** Levi Cassell 
* **Directors/Blowers:** Over, Robinson, and Crimmel .

This structure remained relatively stable through the 1870s, providing the continuity necessary for the company to expand its product lines and market share. While the company is frequently referred to as "Belmont Glass Company" in secondary literature and some period advertisements, "Belmont Glass Works" became the dominant trade name, particularly after 1888 .

**3\. Production Dynamics: From Chimneys to Crystal**

### 3.1 The Staple Trade: Lamp Chimneys
In its initial phase (1866–1870), the factory’s primary output was **lamp chimneys**.8 In the decades before rural electrification, the kerosene lamp was the standard for domestic lighting. The glass chimney, which protected the flame and induced the draft necessary for a bright, smokeless burn, was a consumable commodity. They were fragile, subject to thermal shock, and required frequent replacement. For a new glasshouse, chimneys provided a steady, high-volume baseline of revenue that allowed the firm to refine its furnace operations and train its workforce.

### 3.2 The Pivot to Pressed Tableware
As the company matured, it pivoted toward higher-margin goods. By 1877, trade publications and company letterheads listed a diversified product mix: "table ware, lamps, \[and\] stationers glass ware" . This transition marked Belmont's entry into the competitive world of **Early American Pattern Glass (EAPG)**.

EAPG was a phenomenon of the industrial revolution. It was "pressed" glass, formed by plunging a metal plunger into a mold filled with molten glass. This process allowed for the mass production of intricate designs that mimicked the look of expensive cut crystal. Belmont Glass Works excelled in this medium, leveraging its proprietary mold-making capabilities to produce patterns of exceptional complexity.

### 3.3 The Role of Chemistry: Manganese and "Sun-Purple" Glass
Belmont, like many of its contemporaries, utilized a specific chemical formula for its clear glass. The sand available in the Ohio Valley often contained iron impurities, which naturally tinted the glass a "coke-bottle" green. To counteract this, glassmakers added **Manganese Dioxide** to the batch. The manganese acted as a decolorizer, neutralizing the green hue and rendering the glass crystal clear.

However, this chemical solution came with a delayed reaction. When glass containing manganese is exposed to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight over nearly a century, a photochemical reaction occurs. The manganese oxidizes, slowly turning the glass a faint amethyst or purple color. Today, collectors prize this "sun-purple" tint as a hallmark of authenticity, distinguishing original Belmont production from modern reproductions that use selenium or other decolorizers .

**4\. Center of Excellence: The Belmont Mold Shop**

### 4.1 Vertical Integration
One of the most distinguishing features of the Belmont Glass Works was its vertical integration. While many glass factories outsourced the production of their iron molds to independent foundries, Belmont operated its own foundry and mold shop as early as 1870 .

The mold is the most critical capital asset in pressed glass production. It determines the shape, the pattern, and the surface finish of the final product. By controlling this process in-house, Belmont could:

1. **Protect Intellectual Property:** New designs could be kept secret until launch. 
2. **Ensure Quality Control:** The fit and finish of the mold parts (the "joint lines") could be maintained to higher standards. 
3. **Innovate Rapidly:** Modifications to patterns (such as adding the "skirt" to the Royal pattern to create Venus) could be executed quickly.

### 4.2 The OEM Strategy
Remarkably, Belmont’s mold shop was so proficient that it functioned as an Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) for the broader industry. Historical records confirm that Belmont "chipped" (the term for carving the design into the iron) molds for some of the largest names in American glass, including:

* **McKee & Brothers** (Pittsburgh) 
* **Crystal Glass Company** (Bridgeport, OH) 
* **Central Glass Company** (Wheeling, WV) 
* **Elson Glass Company** 
* **Gillinder Brothers** (Philadelphia) 
* **Fostoria Glass Company**.9

This activity implies that Belmont’s machinists were among the elite of the trade. Producing molds for competitors was a double-edged sword: it generated immediate revenue but also equipped rival firms with the tools to compete. However, it also suggests that Belmont viewed itself as a hub of the Bellaire industrial ecosystem, deeply integrated into the supply chains of its neighbors.

**5\. Artistic Output: A Definitive Catalog of Belmont Patterns**

The artistic legacy of Belmont Glass Works is preserved in its patterns. Unlike the utilitarian chimneys of its early years, these designs were intended to grace the Victorian dining table, serving as affordable luxuries for the American middle class.

### 5.1 The "Royal" and "Venus" Line (c. 1881–1883)
The **"Royal"** pattern (also known as Belmont’s No. 1 or Royal Lady) is perhaps the company's most iconic design. Introduced around 1881, the pattern is characterized by its elegance and distinctive **ball finials** and feet .

* **Design Evolution:** The popularity of the Royal pattern led to a variation introduced in 1883 known as **"Venus"** (No. 2). This iteration retained the core aesthetic but added a "skirted base" and utilized a more conventional finial, likely to differentiate the line or address durability issues with the original ball feet . 
* **Intellectual Property:** The design was significant enough to warrant a patent, filed by **William Fox**.8 This legal protection underscores the commercial value attached to these proprietary designs.

### 5.2 Pattern No. 100: "Daisy & Button" (1886)
While the "Daisy & Button" motif was a generic industry standard produced by dozens of factories, Belmont’s interpretation (Pattern No. 100\) is widely regarded by collectors as one of the most ornate and technically ambitious versions ever produced .

The Technical Marvel of the Covered Compote: 
The covered compote in the Daisy & Button line serves as a masterclass in 19th-century mold engineering. The piece was too complex to be pressed in a single operation. Instead, it was constructed as a composite:

* **The Bowl and Pedestal:** These were pressed separately and then joined while still hot using a "wafer" of molten glass—a technique requiring precise temperature control to ensure a permanent bond without cracking. 
* **The Rim:** Applied separately to the top of the bowl. 
* **The Lid:** Unique to Belmont, the pattern on the lid was pressed on the *inside* surface. This created a smooth exterior that was easier to clean while maintaining the optical brilliance of the pattern through the glass. The finial (a round knob with a bar) was applied separately .

Color Palette: 
Belmont produced the Daisy & Button line in a vibrant array of colors, capitalizing on the Victorian craze for colored glass.

* **Canary (Vaseline):** This yellow-green glass contains uranium oxide, which causes it to fluoresce bright green under ultraviolet light. 
* **Amber and Blue:** Rich, deep tones that complemented the heavy relief of the pattern .

### 5.3 Novelties and Commemoratives
Belmont also catered to the whimsy of the market through the production of "novelties"—small, often humorous or commemorative items.

* **Emperor William Beer Mug:** Following the unification of Germany in 1871, Belmont produced a beer mug featuring the likeness of Emperor William I of Prussia. This item likely appealed to the large German-American population in the Ohio Valley and the Midwest . 
* **Figural Salt Shakers:** The company produced salt shakers in various figural shapes, a popular collectible category .

### 5.4 Other Notable Patterns
* **Dewberry (c. 1870):** A naturalistic pattern patented by **Stephen Hipkins Jr.**.8 
* **Swan (c. 1873/1884):** Reflecting the Victorian fascination with nature, this pattern featured swan motifs, likely on covered dishes . 
* **Giant Bull's Eye (No. 151):** Also known as "Excelsior," this was a heavy, geometric pattern often used for barware due to its durability and optical qualities . 
* **Aida (c. 1880s):** A crystal pattern that showcased the clarity of the company’s lead-free glass .

**6\. The "Racine" Misattribution: A Case Study in Identification**

In the field of Early American Pattern Glass, attribution is often complicated by lost records and the recycling of pattern names. A persistent error in modern database queries and collector circles is the association of the name **"Racine"** with Belmont Glass Works. Extensive analysis of the available evidence confirms that **no such pattern exists** in the Belmont catalog. This misattribution stems from three distinct sources of confusion:

### 6.1 The Metalware Confusion
The **Racine Silver Plate Company** was a manufacturer of silver-plated tablewares, including caster sets (wire or metal frames holding glass cruets for oil, vinegar, and spices). Belmont Glass Works likely supplied the glass bottles for these sets. Collectors finding a set marked "Racine" on the metal base often erroneously attribute the glass pattern to a "Racine" line by Belmont. In reality, the glass is often a standard Belmont pattern (like Daisy & Button) sitting in a holder made by the Racine Silver Plate Co..12

### 6.2 The Horlick's Jar Connection
The city of **Racine, Wisconsin**, was home to the **Horlick's Malted Milk** company. Horlick's used high-quality glass jars, often embossed with "Racine, Wis," to package their powder. These jars are frequently collected alongside EAPG. The proximity of "Racine" jars and Belmont glass in antique listings has led to a conflation of the city of origin with a pattern name .

### 6.3 The Bavarian Porcelain Factor
"Racine" is a documented pattern name for Bavarian china produced by **Hutschenreuther** (often marked "Racine Bavaria"). These ceramics are often sold by the same dealers who sell EAPG, leading to keyword cross-contamination in auction listings .

**Conclusion on Racine:** There is no evidence in primary source material (catalogs, patents, or trade journals) to support the existence of a Belmont "Racine" pattern. The correct attribution for the company's premier line is "Royal" or "Venus."

**7\. Biographical Profiles: The Human Element**

The history of Belmont Glass Works is inextricably linked to the biographies of the men who built it. Their lives offer a window into the social history of the 19th-century industrial workforce.

### 7.1 Henry Crimmel: Soldier, Craftsman, Manager
**Henry Crimmel (1844–1917)** stands as a titan in the history of Ohio glass. Born in Hesse, Germany, Crimmel emigrated to the United States as a child. He served in the American Civil War, a defining experience for his generation. Upon returning to civilian life, he entered the glass trade, rising from a floor worker to a master craftsman and eventually management.

Crimmel served as the plant manager for Belmont Glass Works during its final operational years. He was not merely an administrator; he was an inventor, securing a patent in 1892 for a resealable bottle stopper . His expertise was such that when Belmont closed, he did not retire. Instead, he became a founding figure in the **Novelty Glass Company** of Fostoria and later the **Sneath Glass Company**, following the industry as it migrated west to the gas fields . His brother, **Jacob Crimmel**, also worked at Belmont and became a seminal figure in labor history as a founder of the **American Flint Glass Workers' Union (AFGWU)**, writing extensively for the union journal *American Flint*.2

### 7.2 James S. Gill and the Ancillary Industries
**James S. Gill** represents the technical entrepreneur. One of the original 1868 incorporators, Gill remained a director until 1884\. His departure was significant: he left to establish the **J. S. Gill Glass Pot Company**.5

Glass pots are the large clay crucibles in which the glass batch is melted inside the furnace. They are consumable items with a short lifespan, requiring specialized clay and a months-long drying and firing process. By establishing a dedicated pot factory, Gill signaled the maturation of the Bellaire glass economy; the industry had grown large enough to support specialized supplier firms. His son, **William X. Gill**, followed him into the trade, managing the pot factory after James's death in 1889 .

**8\. The Energy Crisis and the Gas Boom (1888–1890)**

The demise of Belmont Glass Works was not caused by product failure or labor strife, but by a seismic shift in the economics of energy.

### 8.1 Coal vs. Gas
For its first two decades, Belmont relied on the coal mined in the surrounding hills. Coal provided a steady, hot flame, but it was dirty (leaving soot on the glass) and required manual stoking. In the late 1880s, massive reservoirs of **natural gas** were discovered in Northwest Ohio (around Findlay and Toledo).

Natural gas was a miracle fuel for glassmakers. It was clean, burned hotter than coal, and, most importantly, it was incredibly cheap—often offered for free or at flat rates by municipalities eager to attract industry.

### 8.2 The Economic Squeeze
Factories located in the "Gas Belt" (Northwest Ohio and Indiana) could produce glass at a fraction of the cost of the coal-dependent river factories in Bellaire. By January 1890, the strain on Belmont was evident. Trade reports noted that while Belmont produced "one of the finest lines of tableware in the country," it was forced to slash prices to compete with the gas-fueled plants. As a result, the company paid no dividends for the 1889 fiscal year .

The board of directors faced a stark choice: invest massive capital to drill for local gas (which was uncertain) or liquidate while the assets still held value.

**9\. Dissolution and Diaspora (1890–1893)**

### 9.1 The Closure (June 1890\)
In June 1890, the shareholders voted to cease operations. The closure was an orderly liquidation. The machinery and inventory were sold off, and the workforce began to scatter .

### 9.2 The Dispersal of the Molds
The most valuable assets—the molds—were purchased by former competitors. This dispersal explains why Belmont patterns appear in the catalogs of other companies after 1890:

* **Crystal Glass Company** (Bridgeport, OH) acquired a significant portion of the mold inventory. 
* **Central Glass Company** also purchased molds.

This transfer of intellectual property ensured the survival of the designs, even as the company that created them vanished .

### 9.3 From Glass to Steel
The physical plant did not survive. The buildings were demolished, and by 1893, the site at 34th and Hamilton Streets was redeveloped by the **Novelty Stamping Company**, a metalworking firm. This transition mirrored the broader industrial trend of the region, as the steel and metal fabrication industries began to eclipse glass manufacturing in the Ohio Valley .

**10\. Conclusion**

The Belmont Glass Works stands as a microcosm of the American industrial experience in the Gilded Age. Born from the cooperative spirit of returning Civil War veterans, it helped transform Bellaire into the "Glass City," setting standards of excellence in mold making and design that rippled throughout the industry. Its "Royal" and "Daisy & Button" patterns remain enduring icons of Victorian taste, technically sophisticated and artistically vibrant.

However, Belmont’s history is also a cautionary tale of technological disruption. The company survived fire and flood, but it could not survive the economic geography of the Gas Boom. When the center of gravity for glass manufacturing shifted to the natural gas fields of Northwest Ohio, Belmont, tethered to the coal economy of the river, was left behind. Yet, through the migration of men like Henry Crimmel and the preservation of its molds by rival firms, the DNA of Belmont Glass Works survived, woven into the fabric of the American glass tradition.

The popularity of the Royal pattern led to a variation introduced in 1883 known as "Venus" (No. 2).
The "Venus" pattern retained the core aesthetic of the Royal pattern but added a "skirted base" and utilized a more conventional finial.
The design was significant enough to warrant a patent, filed by William Fox.
The "Daisy & Button" motif was a generic industry standard produced by dozens of factories.
Belmont’s interpretation of the "Daisy & Button" motif (Pattern No. 100) is widely regarded by collectors as one of the most ornate and technically ambitious versions ever produced.
The covered compote in the Daisy & Button line serves as a masterclass in 19th-century mold engineering.
The covered compote piece was too complex to be pressed in a single operation.
The covered compote was constructed as a composite.
The bowl and pedestal of the covered compote were pressed separately and then joined while still hot using a "wafer" of molten glass.
The technique of joining the bowl and pedestal required precise temperature control to ensure a permanent bond without cracking.
The rim of the covered compote was applied separately to the top of the bowl.
Unique to Belmont, the pattern on the lid of the covered compote was pressed on the *inside* surface.
Pressing the pattern on the inside surface of the lid created a smooth exterior that was easier to clean.
Pressing the pattern on the inside surface of the lid maintained the optical brilliance of the pattern through the glass.
The finial (a round knob with a bar) of the covered compote was applied separately.
Belmont produced the Daisy & Button line in a vibrant array of colors.
Canary (Vaseline) glass contains uranium oxide.
Uranium oxide causes Canary (Vaseline) glass to fluoresce bright green under ultraviolet light.
Amber and Blue were rich, deep tones that complemented the heavy relief of the Daisy & Button pattern.
Following the unification of Germany in 1871, Belmont produced a beer mug featuring the likeness of Emperor William I of Prussia.
The company produced salt shakers in various figural shapes.
Dewberry (c. 1870) is a naturalistic pattern patented by Stephen Hipkins Jr.
Swan (c. 1873/1884) is a pattern that featured swan motifs, likely on covered dishes.
Giant Bull's Eye (No. 151) is also known as "Excelsior".
Giant Bull's Eye (No. 151) was a heavy, geometric pattern often used for barware due to its durability and optical qualities.
Aida (c. 1880s) is a crystal pattern that showcased the clarity of the company’s lead-free glass.
A persistent error in modern database queries and collector circles is the association of the name "Racine" with Belmont Glass Works.
Extensive analysis of the available evidence confirms that no such pattern as "Racine" exists in the Belmont catalog.
The Racine Silver Plate Company was a manufacturer of silver-plated tablewares, including caster sets.
Belmont Glass Works likely supplied the glass bottles for caster sets made by the Racine Silver Plate Company.
Collectors finding a set marked "Racine" on the metal base often erroneously attribute the glass pattern to a "Racine" line by Belmont.
The glass in sets marked "Racine" on the metal base is often a standard Belmont pattern (like Daisy & Button) sitting in a holder made by the Racine Silver Plate Co.
The city of Racine, Wisconsin, was home to the Horlick's Malted Milk company.
Horlick's used high-quality glass jars, often embossed with "Racine, Wis," to package their powder.
These Horlick's jars are frequently collected alongside EAPG.
The proximity of "Racine" jars and Belmont glass in antique listings has led to a conflation of the city of origin with a pattern name.
"Racine" is a documented pattern name for Bavarian china produced by Hutschenreuther.
Hutschenreuther Bavarian china is often marked "Racine Bavaria".
These ceramics are often sold by the same dealers who sell EAPG, leading to keyword cross-contamination in auction listings.
There is no evidence in primary source material (catalogs, patents, or trade journals) to support the existence of a Belmont "Racine" pattern.
The correct attribution for Belmont Glass Works' premier line is "Royal" or "Venus."
Henry Crimmel (1844–1917) stands as a titan in the history of Ohio glass.
Henry Crimmel was born in Hesse, Germany.
Henry Crimmel emigrated to the United States as a child.
Henry Crimmel served in the American Civil War.
Upon returning to civilian life, Henry Crimmel entered the glass trade, rising from a floor worker to a master craftsman and eventually management.
Crimmel served as the plant manager for Belmont Glass Works during its final operational years.
Crimmel was an inventor, securing a patent in 1892 for a resealable bottle stopper.
When Belmont closed, Henry Crimmel became a founding figure in the Novelty Glass Company of Fostoria.
Henry Crimmel later became a founding figure in the Sneath Glass Company.
Henry Crimmel's brother, Jacob Crimmel, also worked at Belmont.
Jacob Crimmel became a seminal figure in labor history as a founder of the American Flint Glass Workers' Union (AFGWU).
Jacob Crimmel wrote extensively for the union journal *American Flint*.
James S. Gill was one of the original 1868 incorporators.
James S. Gill remained a director until 1884.
James S. Gill left to establish the J. S. Gill Glass Pot Company.
Glass pots are the large clay crucibles in which the glass batch is melted inside the furnace.
Glass pots are consumable items with a short lifespan.
Glass pots require specialized clay and a months-long drying and firing process.
By establishing a dedicated pot factory, Gill signaled the maturation of the Bellaire glass economy.
The Bellaire glass industry had grown large enough to support specialized supplier firms.
James S. Gill's son, William X. Gill, followed him into the trade.
William X. Gill managed the pot factory after James's death in 1889.
For its first two decades, Belmont relied on the coal mined in the surrounding hills.
Coal provided a steady, hot flame, but it was dirty (leaving soot on the glass) and required manual stoking.
In the late 1880s, massive reservoirs of natural gas were discovered in Northwest Ohio (around Findlay and Toledo).
Natural gas was a miracle fuel for glassmakers.
Natural gas was clean, burned hotter than coal, and was incredibly cheap.
Natural gas was often offered for free or at flat rates by municipalities eager to attract industry.
Factories located in the "Gas Belt" (Northwest Ohio and Indiana) could produce glass at a fraction of the cost of the coal-dependent river factories in Bellaire.
By January 1890, the strain on Belmont was evident.
Trade reports noted that while Belmont produced "one of the finest lines of tableware in the country," it was forced to slash prices to compete with the gas-fueled plants.
As a result, the company paid no dividends for the 1889 fiscal year.
In June 1890, the shareholders voted to cease operations.
The closure was an orderly liquidation.
The machinery and inventory were sold off, and the workforce began to scatter.
The most valuable assets—the molds—were purchased by former competitors.
This dispersal explains why Belmont patterns appear in the catalogs of other companies after 1890.
Crystal Glass Company (Bridgeport, OH) acquired a significant portion of the mold inventory.
Central Glass Company also purchased molds.
This transfer of intellectual property ensured the survival of the designs, even as the company that created them vanished.
The physical plant did not survive.
The buildings were demolished.
By 1893, the site at 34th and Hamilton Streets was redeveloped by the Novelty Stamping Company, a metalworking firm.
This transition mirrored the broader industrial trend of the region, as the steel and metal fabrication industries began to eclipse glass manufacturing in the Ohio Valley.

3.title: Bellaire Goblet Company
3.content:
Bellaire Goblet Company| Industry | [Glass manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass") |
| --- |
| Founded | 1876 |
| Founder | E. G. Morgan, C. H. Over, Henry Carr, John Robinson, M. L. Blackburn, and W. A. Gorby |
| Defunct | 1891 |
| Successor | Factory M of [U.S. Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Glass_Company "United States Glass Company")(closed 1893) |
| Headquarters | [Bellaire, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire,_Ohio "Bellaire, Ohio")1876-1888; [Findlay, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Findlay,_Ohio "Findlay, Ohio")1888-1891 |
| Key people | John Robinson, Charles Henry Over |
| Products | [goblets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stemware "Stemware"), [tableware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tableware "Tableware") |
| Number of employees | 312 (1888) |

The **Bellaire Goblet Company** (sometimes mislabeled as Bellaire Goblet Works) was the largest manufacturer of goblets (glass [stemware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stemware "Stemware")) in the United States during the 1880s. Its original glass plant was located in [Bellaire, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire,_Ohio "Bellaire, Ohio"), a town that earned the nickname "Glass City" because of its many glass factories. Bellaire Goblet Company was part of Ohio's "Glass City" on the east side of the state, and later moved to the other side of the state to participate in [Northwest Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Ohio "Northwest Ohio")'s "Gas Boom". It also became part of a large glass [trust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trust_(business) "Trust (business)").

The company was incorporated on July 31, 1876, by experienced glass makers from the [Belmont Glass Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works "Belmont Glass Works"), which was Bellaire's first glass manufacturer. Operations for Bellaire Goblet started later in the year. By 1879 the company was exporting goods to Europe, South America, and Australia, and it expanded production capacity by leasing an additional glass works in town. Bellaire had what glass companies and other manufacturers needed: a good transportation infrastructure, a good labor supply, and plenty of coal for fuel.

In 1886 Northwest Ohio began a "gas boom" with the discovery of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") near the small community of [Findlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Findlay,_Ohio "Findlay, Ohio"). Local businessmen used incentives such as free land, cash, and low-cost natural gas to lure energy–intensive manufacturers to set up operations there. Bellaire Goblet Company moved to Findlay in 1888. The company kept the name "Bellaire" because of the brand recognition already associated with that name. During the next few years Northwest Ohio began having gas shortages in addition to the country's economic [recession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recession "Recession"), and this put financial hardship on companies that relied on large quantities of fuel for their manufacturing process. In 1891 Bellaire Goblet Company was sold to a glass trust named [United States Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Glass_Company "United States Glass Company") and became known as the trust's "**Factory M**". The Factory M plant was closed permanently in January 1893 when it had no fuel for its furnaces after the town stopped providing natural gas. The plant was sold to a non–glass company in 1894.

Glass is made by starting with a [batch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass_batch_calculation "Glass batch calculation") of ingredients, melting it together, forming the glass product, and gradually cooling it. The batch of ingredients is dominated by sand, which contains [silica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silicon_dioxide "Silicon dioxide").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CorningHow-1) The batch is placed inside a pot or tank that is heated by a furnace to roughly 3090°F (1700°C).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CorningHow-1) The melted batch is typically shaped into the glass product (other than [plate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plate_glass "Plate glass") and window glass) by either a [blowing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glassblowing "Glassblowing") or [pressing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pressed_glass "Pressed glass") it into a [mold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molding_(process) "Molding (process)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Weeks45-2) The glass product must then be cooled gradually ([annealed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annealing_(glass) "Annealing (glass)")), or else it could easily break.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CorningAnnealing-3) An oven used for annealing is called a [lehr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lehr_(glassmaking) "Lehr (glassmaking)").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CorningLehr-4) Because most glass plants melted their ingredients in a pot during the 1880s, a plant's number of pots was often used to describe capacity.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Owens25-26-5) One of the major expenses for the glass factories is fuel for the furnace.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-DOC12-6) Wood and coal have long been used as fuel for glassmaking. An alternative fuel, natural gas, became a desirable fuel for making glass because it is clean, gives a uniform heat, is easier to control, and melts the batch of ingredients faster.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-WoodCoalGas-7)

[![Image 1: map of Ohio showing two major glass making centers](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c8/OhioGlassMakingCenters1888BellaireFindlay.png/250px-OhioGlassMakingCenters1888BellaireFindlay.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OhioGlassMakingCenters1888BellaireFindlay.png)

Old glass making center circled on east side (dot marks Bellaire), new center on northwest side (dot marks Findlay)

[Belmont County, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_County,_Ohio "Belmont County, Ohio"), is located in the Ohio coal belt on the eastern side of the state.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Belmont-8) One of the county's [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") communities is [Bellaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire,_Ohio "Bellaire, Ohio"). At one time, steamships traveling down the Ohio River knew Bellaire as the last stop for coal until [Cincinnati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Ohio "Cincinnati, Ohio").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bellaire7-9) Bellaire had ten coal mines in the hills adjacent to the town.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Howe321-10) An 1873 map shows the [Central Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Ohio_Railroad "Central Ohio Railroad") entering Bellaire from the west, and the [Cleveland and Pittsburgh Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Line_(Norfolk_Southern) "Cleveland Line (Norfolk Southern)") entering Bellaire from the north.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Ohio1873map-11) The Central Ohio Railroad was Bellaire's first, and it connected Bellaire with Columbus, Ohio. The line began being operated by the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad in 1865. The Cleveland and Pittsburgh Railroad eventually became controlled by the [Pennsylvania Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania_Railroad "Pennsylvania Railroad").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-McKelvey171-12) In addition to its railroads, the [National Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Road "National Road") ran through Bellaire.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-McKelvey68-13) A few miles upriver was the city of [Wheeling, West Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling,_West_Virginia "Wheeling, West Virginia"), which was an early glass producing center in what was at that time, the American "[west](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midwestern_United_States "Midwestern United States")". Glass was first made in Wheeling in the 1820s, and one of the larger glass works in the United States, [J. H. Hobbs, Brockunier and Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._H._Hobbs,_Brockunier_and_Company "J. H. Hobbs, Brockunier and Company"), was still operating there in the 1880s.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Weeks78-79-14)

Given Bellaire's transportation resources, fuel resource, and experienced workforce nearby, the town was an excellent location for a glass manufacturing plant. The [Belmont Glass Works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works "Belmont Glass Works"), which began production in 1866, was Bellaire's first of many glass plants and the second in Belmont County.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-BellaireGood-15) For the period of 1870 to 1885, Bellaire's nickname was "Glass City" because of its numerous glass factories and the large amount of capital invested in them.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-McKelvey170-16) By 1880, Belmont County ranked sixth in the value of glass produced among the nation's counties, and the state of Ohio ranked fourth.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Weeks1115-17) Glass manufacturers inspected in Bellaire in 1888 (includes makers of bottles, fruit jars, glassware, lantern globes and window glass) were: Rodefer Brothers, Aetna Glass Manufacturing, Bellaire Fruit Jar, Union Window Glass Works, Crystal Window Glass, Lantern Globe, Bellaire Bottle, Belmont Glass Works, Bellaire Window Glass Works, Enterprise Window Glass, and Bridgeport Glass.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-SOODorn37-38-18) Partially caused by the gas boom in Northwest Ohio, Bellaire had only three glass furnaces in 1891 after a peak of 17 in 1884.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CGJ19031217-19)

### Northwest Ohio gas boom

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bellaire_Goblet_Company&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Northwest Ohio gas boom")]

In early 1886, a major discovery of [natural gas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_gas "Natural gas") occurred in Northwest Ohio near the small village of [Findlay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Findlay,_Ohio "Findlay, Ohio").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-FindlayGas-20) Although small natural gas [wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_well "Oil well") had been drilled in the area earlier, the well drilled on property owned by Louis Karg was much more productive than those drilled before. Soon, many more wells were drilled, and the area experienced an [economic boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boom_and_bust "Boom and bust") as gas workers, businesses, and factories were drawn to the area.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-FindlayGas-20) In 1888, Findlay community leaders, assuming the supply of natural gas was unlimited, started a campaign to lure more manufacturing plants to the area. Incentives to relocate to Findlay included free natural gas, free land, and cash.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette26-21) These incentives were especially attractive to glass manufacturers, since the glass manufacturing process is energy-intensive.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-EIAglass-22)

The gas boom in Northwest Ohio enabled the state to improve its national ranking as a manufacturer of glass (based on value of product) from 4th in 1880 to 2nd in 1890.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Census315-23) Over 70 glass companies operated in northwest Ohio between 1880 and the early 20th century.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette28-24) However, Northwest Ohio’s gas boom lasted less than five years. By 1890, the region was experiencing difficulty with its gas supply, and many manufacturers were already shutting down, using alternative fuels, or considering relocating.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette28-24)

Production in Bellaire
----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bellaire_Goblet_Company&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Production in Bellaire")]

[![Image 2: map of large glass works with storage and railroad track for coal](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/Bellaire_Goblet_Co_insurance_map_1884.png/500px-Bellaire_Goblet_Co_insurance_map_1884.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bellaire_Goblet_Co_insurance_map_1884.png)

The main Bellaire Goblet glass works in Bellaire during 1884

The Bellaire Goblet Company (sometimes mislabeled as Bellaire Goblet Works) received its charter from the state of Ohio on July 31, 1876.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bell190-25) It was organized in the fall by E. G. Morgan, Charles Henry Over, Henry Carr, John Robinson, Melvin L. Blackburn, and William A. Gorby. Morgan was president, Gorby was secretary and treasurer, and Over was manager.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Organization-26) Most of the founders were experienced glass men from the Belmont Glass Works with exception of Morgan, who provided capital.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Cranmer485-27) Robinson and Over had also worked at the J. H. Hobbs, Brockunier and Company before being involved with the Belmont Glass startup.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette57-28) The company's original glass product was exclusively goblets (glass [stemware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stemware "Stemware")).[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Cranmer485-27) Production was conducted using a workforce of about 100 employees working a 10–pot furnace.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Production1-29) The company would eventually expand its products to include [tableware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tableware "Tableware") and pressed stemware.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette57-28)

During the 1870s, [deflation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deflation "Deflation") was an economic issue for manufacturers. One source estimates that [consumer prices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consumer_price_index "Consumer price index") decreased for seven years in that decade, while they remained unchanged for the other three.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-FRBMinnCPI-30) To combat falling prices, manufacturers of similar products formed trade associations, typically known as [holding companies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holding_companies "Holding companies") or [trusts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trusts "Trusts").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GobletTrust-31) (The [Sherman Antitrust Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sherman_Antitrust_Act "Sherman Antitrust Act") was not passed until 1890.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GobletTrust-31)) During February 1877, a cartel named Pittsburgh and Wheeling Goblet Company was formed with the objective of limiting the sale of goblets below prices determined by the "partnership".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GobletTrust-31) Eighteen manufacturers of goblets were part of the trust, and this included a non-union manufacturer: Bellaire Goblet Company.[[Note 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-33) Competitive pressures prevailed, and the group disbanded on September 11, 1877.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GobletTrust-31)

During March 1879, Bellaire Goblet leased (and eventually purchased) an additional glass plant that had an 8–pot furnace. That plant was expanded with the addition of a 14–pot gas furnace.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Cranmer485-27) In September, the company's two factories had a capacity of 7,500 dozen goblets per week—and two months–worth of unfilled orders. They exported to South America, Germany, and Australia. Domestically, half of their product was sold in the eastern United States, especially Boston and New York. St. Louis, Chicago, Cincinnati, and San Francisco were major destinations for goblets in the west.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CC18790910p12-34) The company's employee count was about 150.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CC18790910p12-34)

In 1880, Bellaire Goblet Company had three furnaces with a total capacity of 29 pots.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-OhioBLS181-35) This meant the company had 10 percent of Ohio's glassmaking capacity. It was also the largest of Bellaire's six glass manufacturers, and third largest of the 19 in the state.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-OhioBLS181-182-36) By 1885, the employee count grew to 175 men and boys.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-BC18851015-37) A report for 1887 listed Bellaire Goblet as having 285 employees and as one of eleven glass companies in Bellaire.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Howe320-38) During March 1888, a newspaper noted that there was a "strong probability" that the company would move to Findlay, Ohio.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-BC18880329p3-39)

Production in Findlay
---------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bellaire_Goblet_Company&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Production in Findlay")]

[![Image 3: map of large glass works](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/34/Bellaire_Goblet_Works_Findlay_Ohio_1890.png/500px-Bellaire_Goblet_Works_Findlay_Ohio_1890.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bellaire_Goblet_Works_Findlay_Ohio_1890.png)

Bellaire Goblet glass works in Findlay during 1890

The management of Bellaire Goblet Company decided in March 1888 to move to Findlay, Ohio. A major reason for the move was the incentives: free natural gas for five years (important for the furnaces), free land, and $15,000 cash (equivalent to $524,944 in 2024).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette5659-40)[[Note 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-42) Construction of the glass works began in late April.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette57-28) The new plant had two 15-pot furnaces, and equipment from the Bellaire works was shipped by rail to Findlay.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette57-28) The plant's location in Findlay was on Bolton Avenue (between Davis and College streets) near a switching track from the [Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cincinnati,_Hamilton_and_Dayton_Railway_(1846%E2%80%931917) "Cincinnati, Hamilton and Dayton Railway (1846–1917)").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-LocationWorks-43)

When Bellaire Goblet Company moved to Findlay, it leased its two Bellaire glass works to another glass company.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Cranmer485-27) Charles Henry Over and company president E. G. Morgan decided to not move to Findlay. Melvin L. Blackburn became president while William Gorby continued as secretary and treasurer. John Robinson became plant manager, replacing Over.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette57-28) Some of the Bellaire plant's 300 workers chose to remain in Bellaire and work for the company leasing the Bellaire glass works.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette56-57-44)

Production in the new Findlay glass works began on August 13. The only problems were not factory–related: workers were difficult to find, and housing for the workers was scarce.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette58-45) An inspector's report for 1888 listed the company as employing 250 males, 12 females, and 50 boys.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-SOODorn55-46) Production at the new plant went well and continued into the next year with no major problems.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette58-45)

[![Image 4: newspaper article describing a fire at the Ballaire Goblet glass works in 1889](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/a/ae/BellaireGobletFire1889.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BellaireGobletFire1889.png)

Bellaire Goblet glass works destroyed by fire in 1889

Early in the morning of May 9, 1889, the Bellaire Goblet plant was destroyed by fire in what was called the "most destructive fire in the history of Findlay".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-BigFire-47) The fire destroyed everything except the building's brick walls and furnaces. The total loss was estimated at over $100,000 (equivalent to $3,499,630 in 2024), and insurance covered about $65,000 (equivalent to $2,274,759 in 2024).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-BigFire-47) Although some newspapers said the glass works would be rebuilt at once, management was concerned about the availability of natural gas.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Concerns-48) Even though the company had signed a contract for five years of free gas, the contract was nullified by Findlay's gas producer. Bellaire Goblet was offered a new contract, contingent on the company rebuilding the glass works as soon as possible, for gas at $400 (equivalent to $13,999 in 2024) per year for five years, which would be available if the city had a sufficient supply.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette59-49) The company signed the contract on June 9, 1889, and the rebuild of the glass works began. The company's glassmakers were used as a construction workforce, and the plant resumed full production on August 18, 1889.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette59-49) The Bellaire Goblet Company had a capacity of 30 pots, making it second in capacity among Findlay's twelve glass companies.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GSOp119-50)

In December 1890, gas rates were raised from $400 per year to $3,600 (equivalent to $125,987 in 2024), and the company was notified that if it did not pay at the new rate its gas would be shut off. The company claimed it already had an agreement to pay $400 per year, but the city said the contract was illegal.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette59-60-51) On top of this potential huge increase in fuel costs, the domestic economy had been in recession since July 1890.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-NBERcycles-52) The company sued over the gas price increase—and lost.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette60-53)[[Note 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-55) The unfavorable decision was made in late June 1891, but management was focused on something else. On July 1, 1891, the Bellaire Goblet Company ceased to exist as it became Factory M of the [United States Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Glass_Company "United States Glass Company").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-JoinUSGlass-56)[[Note 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-58)

[![Image 5: advertisement for fancy glassware with list of cities with salesrooms](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/85/Ad_for_United_States_Glass_Co_from_Glass_and_Pottery_World_April_1896_p5.JPG/250px-Ad_for_United_States_Glass_Co_from_Glass_and_Pottery_World_April_1896_p5.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ad_for_United_States_Glass_Co_from_Glass_and_Pottery_World_April_1896_p5.JPG)

U.S. Glass Company advertisement

The objective of the U.S.Glass Company trust was to lower production costs.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-WDI18910630p5-59) Two ways to lower costs were to get concessions from the unions and to use more mechanization.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bredehoft23-60) U.S.Glass preferred to produce glass using the most modern equipment with relatively unskilled workers.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bredehoft8-61) It began construction of large glass works at [Gas City, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gas_City,_Indiana "Gas City, Indiana"), and [Glassport, Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glassport,_Pennsylvania "Glassport, Pennsylvania"), which would be highly automated.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bredehoft24-62) As fuel is another important cost in glassmaking, Gas City was participating in [East Central Indiana's Gas Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_gas_boom "Indiana gas boom"), and Glassport had a coal mine.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GCGfuel-63)

Factory M began operations during August 1891, and it produced many of the original products made when it was Bellaire Goblet Company.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Lechner32-64) U.S. Glass management signed an agreement to pay $2,700 (equivalent to $94,490 in 2024) per year for the plant's natural gas fuel.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette101-65) Factory M produced glass through December 8, 1892, before going on a holiday stop effective December 10.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-ProdStops-66) Findlay's gas supply was very low, and all glass factories in town had switched to other fuel sources with the exception of two factories owned by U.S. Glass—Factory J and Factory M.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette101-65) Factory J was in the process of switching to oil, but was still using gas.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette99-57) Findlay gas trustees warned Factory M that it should immediately convert to oil for its fuel source., and then raised its gas price to $5,040 (equivalent to $176,381 in 2024) per year.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette101-65) On January 12, 1893, after gas was cut off, U.S. Glass announced that it was shutting down Factory J and Factory M permanently.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-PermStop-67) Equipment from Factory M was stored at the empty Factory J, and eventually equipment from both factories was sent to the Gas City plant (Factory U). The Factory M property was sold to a non–glass manufacturer in May 1894, and the Factory J land was sold in 1910.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette99-101-68)

[![Image 6: advertisement for fancy glassware including a pitcher and tumbler](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg/250px-Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg)

Robinson Glass Company advertisement

Charles Henry Over, who did not move to Findlay, started the C. H. Over Glass Company in 1889. The plant was located in [Muncie, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muncie,_Indiana "Muncie, Indiana"), and employed 175 people.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-CHOver-69) William A. Gorby was a trustee for United States Glass Company. After Bellaire Goblet became Factory M, Gorby became a purchasing agent for U.S. Glass in Pittsburgh.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Paquette60-53) John Robinson resigned as plant manager and started the Robinson Glass Company in [Zanesville, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zanesville,_Ohio "Zanesville, Ohio"). M. L. Blackburn joined Robinson Glass in 1892.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Robinson-70)

During the [Economic depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_depression "Economic depression") of 1893 ([Panic of 1893](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panic_of_1893 "Panic of 1893")), United States Glass Company negotiated with the union to change restrictive work rules and equalize wages in unionized and nonunion glass works. The union refused to make concessions, and a "lockout–strike" lasted from October 12, 1893, until January 1897.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Strike-71) During much of that time glass was still made at the two large plants in Gas City and Glassport, and the company did not suffer from significant financial difficulties.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Bredehoft24-62) In 1896, the company was operating six plants: three in Pittsburgh (Factories B,F, and K), and three more in Tiffin, Gas City, and Glassport.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-GPWorld1896May-72)[[Note 5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-75) Some of the other plants were closed permanently during the strike, including four that were destroyed by fire.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-ClosedPermanently-76) The company experienced more strikes in 1913, including at Gas City and Glassport, and reached a settlement where all of its plants became unionized.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-AFvol16p9-77) More plants were closed during the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") in the 1930s. The company filed for bankruptcy in 1962.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire_Goblet_Company#cite_note-Shotwell579-78)

1.title: An Inside Look at The National Imperial Glass Museum - Visit Belmont County
1.content:
The curators and docents of our museums are looking forward to re-opening and safely welcoming visitors. In the meantime, a series of blogs written by our tourism partners will tell the story of how they became involved and give you an inside look at these unique places.

Our second installment is written by Fred Ottoson, the president of the [National Imperial Glass Collector’s Society.](http://www.imperialglass.org/)

[The National Imperial Glass Museum](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museum.htm), 3200 Belmont Street, Bellaire, Ohio, is still closed. As of May 2, 2020, Ohio Governor DeWine mandated that museums “remain closed per existing Stay Safe at Home Orders.”

Perhaps we will soon receive clarity from the Governor as to when we will be permitted to open. However, regardless of that unknown date, we do not plan to open until we can be sure that we can protect the health of Museum staff and visitors.

Meeting that goal will require further planning and procurement of necessary items and having procedures in place for protection of staff and visitors. We must weigh our responsibility for the health of everyone alongside the importance of the Museum to glass and art enthusiasts, history buffs, and the heart and soul of Bellaire and the entire region.

[![Image 1: Glassware and candelabras of varied colors fill a display case](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/4ada38_7eb0a219ac5d4bf49e0b0cd9364bff91~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1480,h_1110,al_c,q_85,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/4ada38_7eb0a219ac5d4bf49e0b0cd9364bff91~mv2.jpg)](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museum.htm)
[Among the many fine museums in Belmont County, the National Imperial Glass Museum is the only glass museum. Nowhere else can one view and appreciate such a vast collection of the magnificent glass made by Imperial. One can also gain insight into the dedication, artistry, skill, and imagination of the outstanding employees of the institution.](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museum.htm)

**_How did I become involved with the National Imperial Glass Museum?_**

My family’s involvement with Imperial Glass began in 1931 when my grandfather Carl Ottoson and his family moved from Chicago to Bellaire. Earl Newton, Imperial’s sales representative in Chicago, recruited my grandfather to be foreman of the cutting shop at the newly reorganized corporation. (Carl worked at that position until his retirement in the 1950s.) My father Axel, having graduated from Senn High School just months earlier, worked at Imperial on and off through the 1930s when he was not at school back in Illinois earning his degree. His steady employment at Imperial began in the early 1940s and continued until his retirement in 1977. Although I did not choose a career in the glass industry, Imperial has always been a part of my life.

Upon my father’s retirement, he and my mother Eleanor became involved with the former Bellaire Glass and Artifact Museum as docents. It was located at a prominent location on old State Route 7 at 4882 Jefferson St. The relocated Route 7 took it, and many other fine properties in the Gravel Hill neighborhood of Bellaire in the late 1980s.

It was a long-time dream of members of the National Imperial Glass Collectors’ Society to have a museum devoted to the people, products, and history of Imperial Glass Corporation. The Society believed that the legacy of the “Big I” deserved preservation in its special place in Bellaire. (Imperial Glass incorporated in 1901, produced its first glass in 1904, and continued production until 1984 when its second bankruptcy forced it into liquidation.)

In the 1990s, many Society members worked and traveled tirelessly to find a suitable location for the Museum. They settled upon the current building at 3200 Belmont St. in Bellaire. Several years of inordinate sacrifice and indefatigable work by many members climaxed on Thursday, June 5, 2003 with a celebratory grand opening.

Having nothing to do with the Museum up to that point, I began my volunteerism that summer as a docent. Several years later, my involvement deepened as I worked with the Museum’s educational program and publicity. I assumed a position on the Board of Trustees that eventually led to my election as president of the Society in 2017. It has been a privilege to serve the Society in many roles with a multitude of wonderful people through these 18 years.

**_What makes the National Imperial Glass Museum unique?_**

Belmont County was home to a plethora of glass manufacturers dating back to 1866 with the founding of the Bellaire’s Belmont Glass Works at the corner of 34th & Hamilton streets. The majority of the county’s glass works and glass decorating companies were in Bellaire, with others located in Bridgeport, Martins Ferry, and Barnesville. In the 1880s, perhaps even earlier, Bellaire became known as the “Glass City”. More glass houses operated in Bellaire than in any other city in the Upper Ohio Valley, including the major manufacturing center of Wheeling, W. Va. Today, one firm stands alone as the most recognizable name associated with the glass industry in Belmont County and Bellaire—Imperial. The Ohio Historic Marker situated in the lawn of the Museum proclaims Imperial to be the “Gem of ‘The Glass City.'”

[![Image 2: Ohio historical marker for Imperial Glass, the Gem of the Glass City](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/4ada38_dc9952c41aca4da89bf8aee19e02d8e6~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_1480,h_1974,al_c,q_90,usm_0.66_1.00_0.01,enc_auto/4ada38_dc9952c41aca4da89bf8aee19e02d8e6~mv2.jpg)](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museum.htm)
[The Ohio Historic Marker situated in the lawn of the Museum proclaims Imperial to be the “Gem of ‘The Glass City.'”](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museum.htm)

Among the many fine museums in Belmont County, the National Imperial Glass Museum is the only glass museum. Although it is located several blocks north of where the factory was located, the aforementioned yard holds special significance. On that lot at the northeast corner of 32nd & Belmont Streets once stood the First National Bank. Beginning in December 1901, Capt. Ed Muhleman, Imperial’s founder, occupied the first office of the company in that building. Over two years later, in February 1904, Imperial made its first glass at the factory located at Belmont & 29th Streets.

Nowhere else can one view and appreciate such a vast collection of the magnificent glass made by Imperial. One can also gain insight into the dedication, artistry, skill, and imagination of the outstanding employees of the institution.

**_Why I feel people should visit the National Imperial Glass Museum._**

The National Imperial Glass Collectors’ Society operates and maintains the National Imperial Glass Museum for the benefit of the visiting public as we attempt to achieve our mission. One can best realize much of that multifaceted mission by paying a visit to the Museum at 3200 Belmont Street in Bellaire, Ohio and taking a leisurely stroll through the various rooms and exhibits.

Of course, the most prominent feature of the Museum is the glass that envelops a visitor almost immediately upon entering. With the multiple and varied exhibits, we wish that visitors come to appreciate the design, manufacture, and marketing of Imperial’s products. One can also view the various photographs of glass workers, whether group pictures or candid shots as they practiced their craft. Any visitor should not only contemplate the artistry and skill that went into the glass, but also the colorful advertising and promotions that Imperial pioneered.

The Society and its docents expect to help the visitor interpret Imperial’s role in the local community, the nation’s industrial history, and its place in home and family life. We have a substantial library of books, catalogs, and videos that the visitor can utilize to crystalize his or her understanding of the importance of Imperial Glass in the twentieth century.

[![Image 3: A woman standing in front of shelves filled with glassware, possibly arranging items](https://static.wixstatic.com/media/4ada38_12cf0e156e304881ab4b2520a51dc75c~mv2.jpg/v1/fill/w_720,h_774,al_c,q_85,enc_auto/4ada38_12cf0e156e304881ab4b2520a51dc75c~mv2.jpg)](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museumgiftshop/museumgift.htm)
[It was a long-time dream of members of the National Imperial Glass Collectors’ Society to have a museum devoted to the people, products, and history of Imperial Glass Corporation.](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museumgiftshop/museumgift.htm)

We have a modest gift shop where we offer genuine Imperial Glass and associated books and catalogs for sale. Gift shop items are also featured on the museum’s website and Facebook page. Should you wish to make purchase, please message us on Facebook, call 740-671-3971, e-mail [info@imperialglass.org,](mailto:info@imperialglass.org) or download an order form from the [website](http://www.imperialglass.org/site/museumgiftshop/museumgift.htm).

The National Imperial Glass Museum is a “cannot miss” destination for glass enthusiasts, history buffs, and connoisseurs of art. Please plan to visit once we open in 2020. At the time of this writing, we have neither a projected opening date nor have we finalized procedures for operation during this current COVID-19 pandemic. Please contact the museum ahead of time to be sure of any mandates that we require upon anyone entering and touring.

Bellaire, Ohio, 1886
--------------------

* * *

"THE GLASS CITY"
----------------

* * *

WHEELING'S YOUNGER SISTER
-------------------------

* * *

### On the Other Side of the Ohio —The Industries of Bellaire —Window Glass, Glassware, Lanterns, Stamped Goods, Wood Working, etc. —A Thriving Place.

* * *

Bellaire is as fairly entitled to be called "the Glass City" as Wheeling to be known as "the Nail City." When the rolling mill was built by Wheeling operatives at Bellaire her industries were few and unimportant. Shortly glass men from here also opened operations in the thriving little town whose future looked bright in view of the completion of the Central Ohio railroad and construction of the railroad bridge over the river. The town has gradually grown to a thriving city, with two daily papers, and her list of manufactures below, in addition to the nail works, makes an impressive show:

**CRYSTAL WINDOW GLASS COMPANY**— President, Dr. R.W. Muhleman; Secretary, A.W. Voegtly; manufactures window glass; factory on Cleveland & Pittsburgh railroad, Fifth ward; was burned in spring of this year, but iron buildings are being rapidly built on same site.

**UNION GLASS COMPANY** —President, Thomas Wetherald; Secretary, C.C. Kelly; manufactures window glass; factory is on Cleveland & Pittsburgh railroad, in the Fifth ward.

**BELLAIRE WINDOW GLASS COMPANY**— President, A.W. Hamilton; Secretary, S.Q. Hamilton. This was the first window glass house built in Bellaire, and now has two furnaces. It is situated on the Ohio river extension of the Cleveland & Pittsburgh Railroad in the First ward.

**ENTERPRISE WINDOW GLASS WORKS**, on the Ohio River extension of the Cleveland & Pittsburgh Railroad, in the First ward. A. Schick, President, and D.J. Smith, Secretary.

**LANTERN GLOBE COMPANY**, on Baltimore & Ohio Railroad, Fourth ward, uses the building originally built by the Goblet Company. President, J.M. Maring; Secretary, Wm. Bergundthal; manufactures lanterns and lamps.

**OHIO LANTERN COMPANY**, office on Union street and factory in the rear, manufactures lanterns and lamps. This is a co-partnership affair composed of A.L. Baron and W.G. Rufer, founded in 1881.

**BUCKEYE LANTERN COMPANY**, on Baltimore & Ohio Railroad in Second ward, occupies the upper story of the old tobacco warehouse, a large brick building built by the State a few years ago. It manufactures lanterns.

**BELLAIRE COOPER SHOPS**, George W. Grodhaus; situated on Baltimore & Ohio railroad, Fourth ward.

**W.W. McCONNELL**, cooper shops, on Ohio Valley extension of Cleveland & Pittsburgh Railroad, in First ward.

**DuBOIS AND McCOY**, plaining mill and lumber yard, occupy new buildings rebuilt after a fire a few years ago, on Baltimore & Ohio railroad, Fourth ward.

**OHIO VALLEY FOUNDRY**, manufacture stoves and make general line of castings. Situated in First ward on Ohio Valley extension of Cleveland & Pittsburgh railroad, and occupy new building of double the capacity of the old works. This was originally started by Messrs. Parkes and Lewis; but now a joint stock company has greatly increased the capacity of the works.

**AETNA GLASS AND MANUFACTURING COMPANY**, situated in the three story brick building of the old Bellaire Implement Works, with glass furnace in the rear, reached by both Baltimore & Ohio railroad and Ohio Valley extension of the the Cleveland & Pittsburgh railroad; manufactures table ware and many fancy articles. In addition to this the company also runs a large foundry and machine shop in the same building. The officers are Wheeling men.

**THE OHIO VALLEY CEMENT WORKS**, of C. Troll's Sons, at Pinch run, manufactures cement from rocks found beneath the hills in that neighborhood.

**BELLAIRE BOTTLE CO.**, the oldest of the Bellaire glass houses, now has two furnaces; is located on the Baltimore & Ohio railroad in the Fourth ward. It was the first concern to use the Wheeling Company's natural gas. Manufactures a general line of table ware, etc.

**RODEFER BROS.**, the old National Glass Works, in the First ward, on the Ohio Valley extension of the Cleveland & Pittsburgh railroad, manufactures tableware, globes, chimneys and vault lights in great variety.

**BELLAIRE GOBLET COMPANY** in First ward on private switch of Ohio Valley extension of C.& P. railroad, occupies works of the old Ohio Glass Company. Manufactured until this season only goblets and tumblers, but now all sorts of pressed ware has been added. President, M.L. Blackburn; Secretary, W.A. Gorby.

**STEWART & WARD, GLOBE FLOUR MILLS, B. & O. AND C. & P. switches, and Thomas Ault & Son**, on Union street, both do large business both at home and abroad. Both have the modern roller process machinery complete.

**THE BELLAIRE STAMPING COMPANY**, occupies large buildings on Baltimore & Ohio Railroad, Third ward; manufactures lanterns, tin ware and ar caps and has grown very much in the last few years, running steadily with few suspension.

**WILLIAM GILL'S** factory for glass house pots in the Fourth ward, has built up a large business and furnishes many of the pots used by the glass houses of the Ohio Valley.

* * *

**Belmont Glass Co.**

A Selective Bibliography

The Rakow Library

_The_ _Belmont Glass Company_ _, also known as the Belmont Glass Works, was one of the first glass factories in_ _[Bellaire, Ohio](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire,\_Ohio)._ _An 1877 drawing of the Belmont Glass Works lists the company's products as "table ware, lamps, [and] stationers glass ware." Belmont Glass began operations in 1866. The company began as a chimney factory, but switched to glass pressed ware for the kitchen and bars. The company also made lamps. While the company is often called the Belmont Glass Works, its name was Belmont Glass Company from 1866 to 1888, and then Belmont Glass Works from 1888 to 1890, when it ceased operations. It should not be confused with the Belmont Tumbler Company, in operation in the 20_ _th_ _century._

_General books on American pressed glass (Revi, Welker, etc.) will have additional information._

Belmont Glass Works, Bellaire, OH, USA. [Collection of papers], Compiled by J. Stanley Brothers. 1866-1892. 1866-1892. 1 folder (26 items) :

Includes a full page ad for "Royal" pattern. Part of a collection of materials collected and organized by J. Stanley Brothers pertaining to the glass industry and glass objects. Includes information copied from books and periodical articles, ads, actual copies of

newspaper and magazine articles, etc. published between the late 19th century and the early 1970s. For this file, almost all of the glass trade journal references are from American Pottery and Glassware Reporter for the period 1880-1885.
