### Bellaire Goblet Company

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Belmont_Glass_Works&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Bellaire Goblet Company")]

Former directors and employees of Belmont Glass Works contributed to the growth of the American glass industry while the company operated and after its closing in 1890. Charles Henry Over left Belmont Glass in 1876 to form the Bellaire Goblet Company, which became nationally known for its tableware products.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Paquette56-84) Joining him were Judge E. G. Morgan, William Gorby, John Robinson, Melvin Blackburn, and Henry Carr. Morgan was the new company's president, Gorby the secretary, C. H. Over the manager, and Robinson the plant superintendent.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-GobletNew-53)[[Note 9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-86) By 1888, their plant employed about 300 people.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Paquette56-84)

[![Image 12: old glassware advertisement showing a pitcher and tumbler](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg/500px-Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Robinson_Glass_Company_advertisement.jpg)

Robinson Glass Company advertisement

In 1888, the Bellaire Goblet Company moved to Findlay, Ohio, to take advantage of the low-cost natural gas. Henry Over decided not to move to Findlay, and instead founded a new window glassworks in [Muncie, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muncie,_Indiana "Muncie, Indiana"): C. H. Over and Company Glass Works.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-OverWorks-87) This glass factory employed about 175 people.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Glass26-88) John Robinson, who had been plant superintendent when working at Belmont Glass, replaced Henry Over as factory manager at Bellaire Goblet.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Paquette57-89)

In 1891, Bellaire Goblet became part of the U.S. Glass Company conglomerate.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Paquette60-90) While William Gorby remained with the parent firm for many years, Robinson eventually resigned. In 1893, Robinson started the Robinson Glass Company in [Zanesville, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zanesville,_Ohio "Zanesville, Ohio").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-RobinsonGlass-91) Financial assistance was provided by additional investors, including Melvin Blackburn—a partner from the Bellaire Goblet Company. The company produced tableware such as jelly glasses, bar goods, and novelties.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Robinson-92)

### Fostoria Glass Company

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Belmont_Glass_Works&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Fostoria Glass Company")]

John and Henry Crimmel were involved with Belmont Glass Works from the start, and their brother Jacob worked there for several periods.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Cook12-14-93)[[Note 10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-95) Henry and Jacob Crimmel moved to [Fostoria, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostoria,_Ohio "Fostoria, Ohio"), in 1887 to help with the startup of the [Fostoria Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostoria_Glass_Company "Fostoria Glass Company").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-FostoriaMove20-96) They both were considered "key craftsmen in the early period" of Fostoria Glass Company, and both had also worked at the Hobbs plant in Wheeling.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Venable174-97) Their “recipes” for various types of glass were used in the early days of the Fostoria Glass Company.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Murray61-98)[[Note 11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-100) Henry Crimmel was also involved with the startups of the [Novelty Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_Glass_Company "Novelty Glass Company") of Fostoria and the [Sneath Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sneath_Glass_Company "Sneath Glass Company") when it relocated to East Central Indiana.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-HenryStartups-101) Jacob Crimmel was one of the founders of the [American Flint Glass Workers' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Flint_Glass_Workers%27_Union "American Flint Glass Workers' Union"), and wrote articles published in the union's journal, _American Flint_.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Works#cite_note-Unnamed26-102)

11.title: Henry Crimmel
11.content:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

| Henry Crimmel |
| --- |
| [![Image 1: Older man with thinning white hair and a mustache is wearing a tweed suit with a bow tie](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Henry_Crimmel_about_1914_closeup.JPG/250px-Henry_Crimmel_about_1914_closeup.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henry_Crimmel_about_1914_closeup.JPG) circa 1914 |
| Born | February 14, 1844 [Hesse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesse "Hesse"), Germany |
| Died | October 10, 1917 [Hartford City, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford_City,_Indiana "Hartford City, Indiana"), US |
| Known for | [Glassmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass"), [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") Veteran |
| Spouse | Catharine Hammond |
| Children | 2 sons, 1 daughter |

**Henry Crimmel** (February 14, 1844 – October 10, 1917) was an American [glassmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glass "Glass") who became well known in Ohio and Indiana. A [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germans "Germans") that came with his family to America at the age of eight years, the [American Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Civil_War "American Civil War") veteran started at the lowest level in glass making, and learned every aspect of the business.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-1) A skilled [glassblower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glassblowing "Glassblowing") known for his glassmaking expertise and the recipient of two patents, he also worked in management in at least three glass factories – and was one of the co-founders of the [Novelty Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_Glass_Company "Novelty Glass Company") (of Fostoria) and the reorganized version of [Sneath Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sneath_Glass_Company "Sneath Glass Company"). He retired with over 50 years in the industry.

Identity and origins
--------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_Crimmel&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Identity and origins")]

In 1852, the Crimmel family [emigrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emigration "Emigration") from the [Hessen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hesse "Hesse") region of what is now Germany to South [Wheeling, Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheeling,_West_Virginia "Wheeling, West Virginia"). Wheeling had a German population that may have attracted the family.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-2) Immigrants from this time period often, upon arrival in the United States, would ride trains to [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh "Pittsburgh"), Pennsylvania, and then ride in boats down the [Ohio River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohio_River "Ohio River") to settle in cities along the way. An alternative route to Wheeling (from [Baltimore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore "Baltimore")) involved the [Baltimore & Ohio Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltimore_%26_Ohio_Railroad "Baltimore & Ohio Railroad") and/or the [National Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Road "National Road").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-3) Although Hessians had been making glass since the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"),[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-4) it is not known if the Crimmel family members learned glassmaking skills in Europe. However, Henry Crimmel's father and both brothers were also glassmakers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-5) Germans were being recruited to work in glass factories during the 1850s. By the 1870s, family members lived across the river from Wheeling in [Bellaire, Ohio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bellaire,_Ohio "Bellaire, Ohio").

[![Image 2: Young man with a serious expression, with short curly hair and wearing a dark button-down shirt](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/Henry_Crimmel_Civl_War.JPG/250px-Henry_Crimmel_Civl_War.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henry_Crimmel_Civl_War.JPG)

Henry Crimmel in uniform about 1862.

On December 20, 1860, the state of [South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Carolina "South Carolina") adopted an ordinance to [secede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession") from the [Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") of the United States, and six more southern states seceded in the next three months. On April 12, 1861, the [Battle of Fort Sumter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Fort_Sumter "Battle of Fort Sumter") marked the start of the American Civil War. More southern states rebelled and voted to secede from the union, including [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia") on April 17, 1861.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-6) These "rebel" states organized themselves into the [Confederate States of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America").

The city of Bellaire, located in Ohio across the Ohio River from the state of Virginia and the city Wheeling, assumed some strategic importance because of the railroads on both sides of the river and the fact that the Ohio River served as the border between the state of Ohio (pro-Union) and the state of Virginia (voted to secede from the Union). Bellaire became a staging area for Ohio and Indiana Union troops to cross into the South and move by [rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railroad "Railroad") using the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad. There was some fear that rebels from Virginia would cross into Ohio through Bellaire. A training camp was located in the city, and numerous soldiers passed through the town to fight in the south.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-7) It is therefore not surprising that 17-year-old Henry Crimmel enlisted to fight in the Civil War. Many of the workers at South Wheeling's Hobbs Glass works also enlisted.

[![Image 3: Monument to Civil War veterans in Blackford County, Indiana, depicting a man carrying another man with a rifle](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Monument_to_Civil_War_Veterans_of_Blackford_County2.JPG/250px-Monument_to_Civil_War_Veterans_of_Blackford_County2.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Monument_to_Civil_War_Veterans_of_Blackford_County2.JPG)

Blackford County Civil War monument in Hartford City, Indiana.

Henry Crimmel was part of Company I of the [Second Virginia Volunteer Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_West_Virginia_Volunteer_Cavalry_Regiment "2nd West Virginia Volunteer Cavalry Regiment"), which fought for the Union instead of the [Confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"). The Second (West) Virginia Cavalry was composed mainly of recruits from Ohio. The governor of Ohio declined to organize this cavalry, so it was organized in Virginia.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-8) It is not extraordinary for someone that lived in southern Ohio (such as Bellaire) to identify with Wheeling, since some of those citizens of Ohio worked on the Virginia side of the river. Although the city of Wheeling was part of the state of [Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virginia "Virginia"), the city is located in the north, and there was dissent in the Wheeling area about [secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secession "Secession").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-9) The western portion of Virginia, which included Wheeling, eventually became a separate state known as West Virginia, which was loyal to the Union.

Henry Crimmel began his military career as a private, and finished as a [bugler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugle_(instrument) "Bugle (instrument)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-10) By the end of the war, Crimmel's cavalry unit was known as Company I of the [2nd Regiment, West Virginia Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2nd_West_Virginia_Volunteer_Cavalry_Regiment "2nd West Virginia Volunteer Cavalry Regiment"). During the war, the Regiment lost a total of 196 men that were killed, mortally wounded, or died from disease. The 2nd Regiment West Virginia Cavalry served in West Virginia, Virginia, and Maryland – including a battle in [Lynchburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Lynchburg "Battle of Lynchburg") against an army under the command of Confederate General [Jubal Early](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jubal_Anderson_Early "Jubal Anderson Early") that involved a total of 40,000 troops. A battle in [Winchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Opequon "Battle of Opequon") (a.k.a. Opequon) matched a total of 54,000 troops under command of General [Philip Sheridan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_Sheridan "Philip Sheridan") for the Union and General Jubal Early for the rebels. This Union victory is considered by many historians to be the most important battle of the [Shenandoah Valley campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valley_Campaigns_of_1864 "Valley Campaigns of 1864").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-11) Crimmel served in the [cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cavalry "Cavalry") from 1861 until November 1864, when he was honorably discharged.

[![Image 4: Engraved names, arranged in alphabetical order, are visible on a light-colored stone surface](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Henry_Crimmel_on_Civil_War_Monument_in_Hartford_City.JPG/250px-Henry_Crimmel_on_Civil_War_Monument_in_Hartford_City.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henry_Crimmel_on_Civil_War_Monument_in_Hartford_City.JPG)

Henry Crimmel's name on Blackford Civil War monument.

After the war, Henry Crimmel joined the [Grand Army of the Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Army_of_the_Republic "Grand Army of the Republic"), an organization for Union Civil War veterans. He was the original officer of the guard for the local chapter.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-12) His name is on at least two monuments honoring veterans of the Civil War. One is located in his original American hometown of Bellaire, Ohio. Eleven of the 41 soldiers listed on the Bellaire monument fought for West Virginia units instead of Ohio. At least two of these West Virginia soldiers (Henry Crimmel and John Robinson) were known to have worked in the glass business.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-13) The other monument with Henry Crimmel's name on it is the Blackford County Civil War monument (see photos), located in [Hartford City, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford_City,_Indiana "Hartford City, Indiana"). Mr. Crimmel spent the last 23 years of his life in Hartford City, and he is buried in the city's main cemetery.

Glassmaking – the early years
-----------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_Crimmel&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Glassmaking – the early years")]

[![Image 5: map showing Belmont County, Bellaire, Wheeling, and the Ohio River](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/RR_Map_of_Belmont_County_1873.jpg/250px-RR_Map_of_Belmont_County_1873.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:RR_Map_of_Belmont_County_1873.jpg)

Bellaire-Wheeling 1873

The Wheeling-Bellaire region was a good location for manufacturing because of its fuel and transportation resources. Bellaire (Belmont County) had coal, railroad service, and the Ohio River. Wheeling also had railroad service and the Ohio River. The National Road went through both cities. The first known glass factory for which Henry Crimmel worked was the [Hobbs works](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._H._Hobbs,_Brockunier_and_Company "J. H. Hobbs, Brockunier and Company") in Wheeling, (West) Virginia.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-14) Glass had been made in Wheeling as early as 1821, and there were three "glass houses" by 1886.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-15) The Hobbs plant had a transportation advantage because it was located very close to the Ohio River. Henry Crimmel's brother Jacob also worked at the Hobbs plant,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-16) and there is a high probability that older brother John also worked at the same plant—simply because there were not many alternatives at the time. Many years later, one of Jacob Crimmel's American Flint magazine articles described working for the Hobbs Glass Works in 1861, meaning that he was about 13 years old when he started working there.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-17) In the 1860s, duties for youngsters just getting started at glass works often involved adding coal and/or wood to furnaces.

All three Crimmel brothers are listed by the 1870 U.S. Census as glassblowers living in different locations in Bellaire, Ohio. Bellaire, Ohio became known as "Glass City" during the period of 1870 to 1885 because of the number of glass factories in the area.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-19) The first glass factory in Bellaire was the [Belmont Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belmont_Glass_Company "Belmont Glass Company") (a.k.a. Belmont Glass Works), and some of the Belmont's founders were former employees of the Hobbs works in Wheeling – including Civil War veteran John Robinson. Both Henry and Jacob Crimmel worked at the Belmont Glass works, and Henry was a manager. Older brother and Bellaire resident John Crimmel is also believed to have worked at that works. The plant began as a maker of chimneys, but changed to a maker of pressed glassware. Some of the well known glassmakers of the West Virginia-Ohio-Indiana area worked there before they gained their fame.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-20) Eventually, the Belmont factory closed in 1890 after an economic recession.

[![Image 6: newspaper brief about Henry Crimmel leaving Bellaire](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/19/BelmontWR18871117p3.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BelmontWR18871117p3.png)

Crimmel left the Belmont Glass Works

Natural gas was discovered in 1887 in the Findley-Tiffin-Fostoria area of Ohio, and this caused many of the glass houses elsewhere to relocate to be near this low-cost resource. The [Fostoria Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fostoria_Glass_Company "Fostoria Glass Company") started in December 1887, and both Henry and Jacob Crimmel were considered important craftsmen in its early years.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-21) Crimmel recipes for various colors of glass are thought to have been used in the early days of this glass works. Several Crimmel family members were involved in the startup of this plant, and Crimmels were also stockholders.

Although Jacob Crimmel would remain with Fostoria Glass through its eventual move to West Virginia, Henry Crimmel became involved with [Novelty Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novelty_Glass_Company "Novelty Glass Company") of Fostoria.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-22) Novelty was located on the original Fostoria site for the Buttler Art Glass Company, which was destroyed by fire in 1889. Henry Crimmel and his son, A. C. Crimmel were among a group of six listed as the "incorporators". Henry Crimmel was the plant manager, while son A. C. Crimmel was the new company's secretary.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-23) The works opened in early 1891, making items such as figurine salt shakers, punch bowls, cups, and other blown-ware. Glass bottles were also one of the plant's products, and in 1892 Henry received a patent for a bottle and stopper combination that could be resealed but not refilled.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-24) The original Novelty Glass Company was short-lived: it became part of the U.S. Glass Company (as Factory T) in mid-1892, and was destroyed by fire in 1893.

Glassmaking – the later years
-----------------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henry_Crimmel&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Glassmaking – the later years")]

[![Image 7: Clear glass oil lamp with a pink base and a clear glass chimney](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Lantern_made_by_Sneath_Glass_Company.jpg/250px-Lantern_made_by_Sneath_Glass_Company.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lantern_made_by_Sneath_Glass_Company.jpg)

Lantern made by Sneath Glass Company

Shortly after the closing of the Novelty Glass Company, Henry Crimmel joined the Sneath Glass Company in Tiffin, Ohio, as plant manager. The Tiffin plant burnt down, but was reorganized using insurance money and a subsidy from a community in Indiana. The new version of the [Sneath Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sneath_Glass_Company "Sneath Glass Company") was led by Henry Crimmel and Ralph Sneath.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-25) Similar to the transformation of Fostoria after the discovery of natural gas in the area, the [Indiana Gas Boom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Gas_Boom "Indiana Gas Boom") in east central Indiana caused many factories to move to Indiana. Sneath Glass relocated to [Hartford City, Indiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hartford_City,_Indiana "Hartford City, Indiana") in 1894, and Henry Crimmel was manager of the new plant. He was also part owner and a member of the company's board of directors.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-26) Mr. Crimmel had about 30 years of experience by then, and he applied his glass-making skills toward making his employees more efficient. Glassblowers at the Sneath plant were aided by a unique system of air hoses that enabled them to be more productive. Henry Crimmel also received another patent in 1904 for a "Glass Drawing Machine" that was an improvement for glass blowing and prevented irregularities in the glass.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-27) The Sneath Glass plant made [lantern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lantern "Lantern") globes and founts during its early years. During the 1905 to 1915 period, the company began to put less emphasis on lantern-related blown-ware, and more production involved glass canisters for portable kitchen cabinets. By 1910, the factory employed about 150 people.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-28)

Glassmaking was a family business for the Crimmels. Brothers John, Henry, and Jacob Crimmel were glassmakers, and at times two or more of them worked at the same plant. One of Henry Crimmel's sons was a partner with his father in the Sneath Glass Company, and two grandsons also worked at the Sneath plant and eventually became part of management. Three of Henry Crimmel's great-grandsons eventually spent time at the plant long after Henry Crimmel's death, and a great-great-grandson worked briefly at [Indiana Glass Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Glass_Company "Indiana Glass Company"). Both John and Jacob Crimmel also had children that worked in the glass business.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-29)

In 1916, Henry Crimmel suffered a [stroke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stroke "Stroke"), and was forced to completely retire. Although he recovered enough to take walks around town, he also had heart trouble. On October 10, 1917, he died from heart failure.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Crimmel#cite_note-30)

Belmont Glass Works is also known as Belmont Glass Company. It was created in 1865 and began production in 1866 as Barnes, Faupel & Co. It was incorporated in 1868 as Belmont Glass Works. Several glass books refer to the entity as "Belmont Glass Company".
